content: 1. If malaria is diagnosed, initiate treatment with an appropriate antimalarial drug. In cases where a blood smear cannot be obtained, treat presumptively for malaria. 2. During confirmed meningococcal meningitis epidemics, lumbar punctures are not required for all children presenting with petechial or purpuric signs, as these are characteristic of meningococcal infection. 3. For children aged 0–23 months with meningitis, treatment should be tailored to the patient’s age, and other potential causes of meningitis should be excluded. 4. For children aged 2–5 years, Neisseria meningitidis is the most likely pathogen, and presumptive treatment is justified. Administer ceftriaxone at 100 mg/kg/day intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) once daily for 5 days in children aged 2 months to 5 years, or for at least 7 days in children aged 0–2 months. 5. Alternatively, administer oily chloramphenicol as a single IM dose of 100 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 3 g). If no improvement is observed after 24 hours, administer a second dose of 100 mg/kg or switch to ceftriaxone. Note that oily chloramphenicol suspension is thick and may be difficult to inject; if this occurs, divide the dose into two injections, one in each buttock. 6. Tuberculous meningitis can present acutely or chronically, with symptoms lasting from 1 day to 9 months. It may manifest with cranial nerve deficits or a more indolent course involving headache, meningismus, and altered mental status. Initial symptoms are often nonspecific, such as headache, vomiting, photophobia, and fever. 7. Suspect tuberculous meningitis if fever persists for 14 days, or for more than 7 days in the presence of a family history of tuberculosis (TB), a chest X-ray suggestive of TB, unconsciousness unresponsive to bacterial meningitis treatment, or known HIV infection or exposure. 8. If tuberculous meningitis is suspected, consult national and international guidelines. Treatment typically involves a 12-month regimen: a four-drug combination (HRZE) for 2 months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 10 months. Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) should be administered in all cases, with the dose tapered over 4–6 weeks. 9. For multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB meningitis, treatment with fluoroquinolones and other second-line drugs should be conducted within a well-functioning MDR TB program and under the guidance of an experienced clinician. Streptomycin is not recommended for children due to risks of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. 10. Cryptococcal meningitis should be considered in older children with known or suspected HIV infection and immunosuppression. Perform a lumbar puncture, as the opening pressure may be elevated, though cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell count, glucose, and protein levels may appear normal. Analyze CSF using India ink preparation or a rapid cryptococcal antigen test if available. 11. Treat cryptococcal meningitis with a combination of amphotericin B and fluconazole. Provide supportive care, including management of seizures and hypoglycemia. 12. In unconscious children, ensure the airway remains open and adequate breathing is maintained. Nurse the child in the recovery position to prevent aspiration, turn the patient every 2 hours, and avoid allowing the child to lie in a wet bed. Monitor for pressure points and provide oxygen therapy if necessary. 13. Children with bacterial meningitis are at risk of brain edema due to inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or fluid overload. Correct dehydration if present, but avoid overhydration. Administer 50–75% of normal daily fluid requirements intravenously during the first 2 days to maintain fluid balance. 14. Provide nutritional support as soon as it is safe. Breastfeed every 3 hours if possible, or provide milk feeds of 15 mL/kg if the child can swallow. If there is a risk of aspiration, continue IV fluids or feed via a nasogastric tube. 15. Monitor the child’s consciousness and vital signs every 3 hours during the first 24 hours, then every 6 hours. At discharge, assess for neurological problems, especially hearing loss, and measure the head circumference in infants. Refer children with neurological damage for physiotherapy and advise mothers on simple passive exercises. 16. Complications during the acute phase of meningitis include seizures, hyponatremia, and subdural effusions, which may cause persistent fever. Long-term complications include sensorineural hearing loss, motor or developmental problems, and epilepsy. 17. Arrange a hearing assessment for all children 1 month after discharge. Advise families about the possibility of secondary meningococcal cases in the household and recommend prompt treatment if symptoms arise. Chemoprophylaxis should be considered for close contacts of meningococcal cases. 18. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease with serious complications, such as blindness in children with pre-existing vitamin A deficiency, and high mortality. It is rare in infants under 3 months of age. 19. Administer oral vitamin A to all children with measles unless they have already received adequate treatment. Dosages are 50,000 IU for children under 6 months, 100,000 IU for those aged 6–11 months, and 200,000 IU for children aged 1–5 years. If eye signs of vitamin A deficiency are present, give a third dose 2–4 weeks after the second dose. 20. Assess the child’s nutritional status by weighing them and plotting the weight on a growth chart. Encourage continued breastfeeding and frequent small meals. Treat mouth ulcers if present and follow nutritional management guidelines. 21. For mild conjunctivitis with clear watery discharge, no treatment is needed. If pus is present, clean the eyes with boiled cotton wool or a clean cloth dipped in clean water, and apply tetracycline eye ointment three times daily for 7 days. Never use steroid ointments. 22. If the child has mouth sores, clean the mouth with salted water at least four times a day. Avoid giving salty, spicy, or hot foods. If mouth sores reduce food or fluid intake, feeding via a nasogastric tube may be required. 23. Septicemia should be considered in a child with acute fever and severe illness when no other cause is identified. It may also occur as a complication of meningitis, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, or other bacterial infections. Common causative agents include Streptococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and enteric Gram-negative bacilli. 24. In areas where meningococcal disease is common, a clinical diagnosis of meningococcal septicemia can be made if petechiae or purpura are present. Investigations may include a full blood count, urinalysis, blood culture, and chest X-rays. 25. Start antibiotics immediately in children suspected of having septicemia.
